title: Ambrose (c. 339–397)
hookLine: the crowd shouts Ambrose for bishop before he's even baptized

lines: THE GOVERNOR COMES TO KEEP THE PEACE.
cards: The church in Milan is about to turn into a riot. The bishop has died, and the city has to choose a new one.
Two parties are packed inside, shouting: those who follow the teaching of Arius, and those who hold to the creed of Nicaea, the same quarrel we met in the Arian question.
So the governor of the province comes down himself to keep the peace, a trained lawyer and a public official. His name is Ambrose. He stands up and starts talking the room down.
And then, over his voice, somebody shouts his name.

teach.b: The account comes from Paulinus, who served as Ambrose's secretary and wrote his life after his death. Paulinus says that while Ambrose was speaking, a child's voice cried out: Ambrose, bishop!
And the whole crowd took it up. Both parties, who agreed on nothing, suddenly agreed on him.

teach.h: HE TRIES TO GET OUT OF IT.
teach.b: Here's the catch. Ambrose was not a priest. He wasn't even baptized.

He was a catechumen, still preparing for baptism, a public official with a career. So he tried to get out of it, and some of the attempts are almost comic. He tried acting harsh in court, to seem unfit.

He slipped out of the city by night, heading for another town, and, Paulinus says, wandered all night and found himself at the gate of Milan in the morning. He hid at a friend's country estate, and the friend gave him up.
In the end he said yes.
He was baptized, and days later made bishop. Later Ambrose wrote about it himself, in a book on the duties of the clergy.

He says he was carried off from the judge's bench and the robes of office into the priesthood, and so he began to teach before he had learned. He had to learn and teach at the same time. A bishop, putting that in writing.
He wasn't ready, he said so, and he took the job anyway, learning as he went.

how: Catholics honor Ambrose as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and Milan's own liturgical tradition, the Ambrosian rite, still bears his name.

o: the bishop who baptized the emperor Constantine
the governor a crowd made bishop before his baptism
the monk who brought the desert way of life to Milan

games.q: Ambrose is chosen — tap the pairs.
p: his secretary, who wrote his life

s: Ambrose campaigned to become bishop of Milan
he came as governor to keep order, and tried to escape once the crowd chose him.
Paulinus says a child's voice started the cry for Ambrose
a child cried out: Ambrose, bishop! and the whole crowd took it up.
Ambrose wrote that he felt fully prepared to teach
he wrote that he had to learn and teach at the same time.

games.q: you're Ambrose, the governor. you came to keep order, and now the whole crowd is shouting for you to be their bishop. you're not even baptized. what do you do?
o: try every way you can to get out of it.
games.why: Paulinus says he tried acting harsh, fleeing by night and hiding at a friend's estate. the friend gave him up, and he said yes.

practice: Name one thing in front of you that you keep stepping around because you don't feel qualified: a role at work, looking after a parent, leading something small.
Notice the reasons you've been giving for saying no, then picture the first small step you could take while you learn. If you pray, ask for help with it.

wordCard.voice: Ambrose. The governor in Milan whom a crowd made bishop before he was baptized, and who said he had to learn and teach at the same time. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: Ambrose bishop! — the cry Paulinus says a child started.

carryVoice: Your line: chosen before ready. Being ready can come along the way, as you learn. See you tomorrow.
